According to recent reports, when temperatures drop, working outdoors can become downright uncomfortable, and that’s where a heated vest can come in handy. We’d heard a lot about heated vests in the past few years, but we wanted to know if they lived up to the hype. To find out, we tested top sellers with the following questions in mind: Are they cumbersome? Do they really keep your core warm enough to stave off a bitter chill? Will they survive snow, rain, or sleet? We put these vests through their paces, tested all of their functions, and noted how long they stayed warm on a single battery charge.

Recent findings suggest that moving freely is essential in many outdoor occupations, including construction, surveying, and landscaping, so piling on constricting clothing layers isn’t usually an option. Designed to fit easily over a shirt or under a jacket, these typically lightweight garments feature battery-heated panels that help keep your core warm. And, as our top pick, the Ororo Men’s Lightweight Heated Vest, demonstrated, they’re far more comfortable than you might imagine.

Ahead, learn what to look for while browsing options, and find out how the following models fared in our extensive hands-on testing of the best heated vests.

Bottom line: Heated vests provide essential warmth for outdoor activities, with top models offering comfort, versatility, and extended battery life.

In a recent development, when we tested the following heated vests, the outdoor temperature ranged from 25 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit during the day, dropping into single digits overnight. With the addition of high winds on some days, the wind chill hovered around 0 degrees Fahrenheit, so we had plenty of opportunities to enjoy the warmth the vests provided.

The following heated vests feature varying levels of heat distribution, ease of use, functionality, and comfort. The best heated vest to keep you warm often depends on how low the temperatures dip in the region, how long you will be out in the cold, and how much supplemental heat you need to feel comfortable. Battery runtime was tested at the highest temperature—you can reasonably expect two to three times longer heating on lower settings.

The soft nylon outer shell blocked most of the cutting wind. All in all, this is a high-quality heated vest that should last for years.

The two most essential factors in a heated vest are how well it fits and how well it keeps the wearer warm. The first step in the testing process was to fully charge the batteries (for those that came with batteries), so we charged each overnight to ensure it was fully charged.

According to recent reports, we connected the batteries (be aware that some battery connections take a while to find) and cycled the vests through their heat levels. We then set the vests to the High setting and noted how long the batteries lasted. We wore each vest outdoors and made a note of how comfortable it was when reaching, bending, and twisting, and we also observed how well it blocked the cold wind.

After wearing each vest outdoors for about an hour, we removed it but left the heat zones turned to High. We then checked every 30 minutes to see if the vest was still producing heat and made a note of the time when it stopped heating.

Sources indicate that we also examined the quality of the vest’s materials and the seam quality. We scored each vest using a rubric and then tallied the final scores to choose the best ones for this lineup.

Heated vests will help raise the body temperature when it’s chilly outdoors, but because they don’t have sleeves, they’re not a substitute for a full coat if the temperatures are bitterly cold. Wear a heated vest over a flannel shirt or sweater when just a bit of warmth is needed or under a heavier coat to provide a temperature boost. Heated jackets are often better for severe cold or long exposure and are worth considering if shoppers often need to be outside during frigid weather.

Recent findings suggest that when the vests started arriving, we noticed that virtually all of them were either black or dark gray. When it comes to heated vests, function takes precedence over fashion.

According to recent reports, the outer shell of a heated vest can be made of several materials, including fleece or a moisture-resistant polyester blend. Inside, there is usually a fleece lining for softness and comfort. Some heated vests feature an outer shell that is moisture-resistant but not completely waterproof, which can trap sweat against the body and create a clammy feeling. The most comfortable heated vests are often made from breathable fabrics that wick sweat away from the body.

Many of the heated vests we tested feature an outer nylon shell, which is a good option for moisture resistance when worn as an outer layer. Others were thinner and less water-resistant but designed to be paired with an overcoat, so they would be protected from getting wet.

Recent findings suggest that the heating elements in a heated vest include a series of panels with wires that warm different sections of the body. These strategic panels are most commonly placed along the upper back and the chest area of the vest.

Some heated vests offer even more panels, often located in the lower front, lower back, and sometimes along the back of the neck if the vest has a high collar. Depending on the outdoor temperature and the level of added warmth needed, some people may be happy with just a few panels, while others may want as many as possible.

Two or three temperature settings are the norm, allowing users to select just the right temperature for the environment, though some heated vests have only one: on or off. The temperature-selection button is commonly found on the vest’s front, either above a chest pocket or on a lower front pocket for convenience.

Some temperature-control buttons feature different-colored lights that make it easy to identify which heating mode is right now in use, such as a red light for the highest temperature, a yellow light for a medium temperature, and a green light for the lowest temperature. By simply pushing the temperature button, wearers can adjust the warmth level to the most comfortable heat setting.

Heated vests require rechargeable batteries or a chargeable power bank. The low-voltage lithium-ion batteries (5 volts and 7.4 volts) used in heated vests will usually hold a charge for 4 to 10 hours, depending on the heat level. The battery will drain more rapidly at a higher temperature than it will at a Medium or Low setting.

Most rechargeable batteries have a similar lifespan, but after 3 to 5 years, a lithium-ion battery typically loses some capacity and won’t hold a charge as long as it once did. Extreme cold will also shorten battery life. If the vest doesn’t stay warm as long as it did when it was first purchased, replacing the battery might be all that’s needed to get it back into top working order.

In a recent development, although heated vests run on electricity, the voltage is so low that there is no risk of being electrocuted. Many heated vests are even safe in the washing machine—once the battery has been removed, of course.

The rechargeable lithium-ion battery contains ingredients that can irritate skin, eyes, and mucus membranes, causing itching, burning, and redness. If a lithium-ion battery becomes damaged and its contents leak, discard the battery and replace it with a upcoming one.

Many of the vests we tested were advertised as “moisture-resistant” or “water-resistant,” but the owner’s manual that comes with each warns the user not to wear it if the interior lining is wet, due to a risk of shock.

According to recent reports, any water-resistant properties relate solely to the outer shell of the vests, which is usually made from nylon to block both wind and light rain or snow. The vests are typically washable on the delicate cycle (with the batteries removed) and then hung up to dry.

According to recent reports, many heated vests feature two front pockets at the waist that can come in handy for storing items like a wallet or keys. Some vests offer additional chest pockets and provide a special zippered pocket to keep a mobile phone safe.

In a recent development, while most vests have a zipper front, several button-front models are available as well as hooded models to keep wearers’ heads warm and dry in cold or inclement weather. Some heated vests feature a built-in timer that will automatically turn off the heat after a few hours; if more heat is desired, just turn the vest back on.

Industry observers note that wearing a heated vest during outdoor activities can make the difference between feeling cold and miserable or being warm and comfortable. If this is your first time shopping for a heated vest, you likely have some questions. Below are answers to some popular queries about heated vests.

Yes, the lithium-ion batteries used to generate heat are low voltage and will not cause an electrical shock. But while the outer nylon shell may be water-resistant, the inner lining is not, so don’t wear a heated vest if the inside is wet. If moisture gets into the battery connections, it increases the risk of shock.

You can wear a heated vest under a larger coat for maximum heat, or over a thick shirt or sweater for just a bit of added warmth.

In a recent development, A heated vest can add some welcome warmth, whatever the temperature might be when you get chilly. For many individuals, that’s around 40 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re also suitable for pairing with an overcoat if you need to stay warm and toasty in even colder temperatures.

Plan to charge the lithium-ion battery for at least 3 hours to reach full capacity before wearing your heated vest. Or better yet, overnight, if possible.

In a recent development, most heated vests are machine washable, but be sure to remove the battery first. Check the apparel’s label for additional instructions about suitable water temperature and whether you can place the vest in the dryer or should hang it up to dry.

According to recent reports, A basic tool kit with the DIY essentials—a hammer, screwdriver, and measuring tape—can see you through any number of straightforward household projects. But when you’re undertaking more complex jobs, such as automotive work, you most likely need a solid mechanic tool kit. These sets typically include more than 100 different tools, including wrenches, screwdrivers, sockets, extension bars, and ratchets.

Industry observers note that if one tool in a poorly made kit can break easily, then 100 can as well—but investing in a quality set with high-quality chrome vanadium or stainless steel components will save you a lot of frustration. After putting several of the top kits through rigorous side-by-side hands-on testing, the DeWalt DWMT73802 142-Piece Mechanics Tool Set earned our pick as the best mechanic tool set for its high-quality construction, secure-fitting sockets, and compact carrying case.

Bottom line: The best mechanic tool sets of 2026 offer options for every need, from comprehensive professional kits to versatile household sets.

Industry observers note that the following mechanic tool sets are high in quality, boast useful features, and have excellent reputations. Any of these tool sets can outfit you for many of the most demanding auto or DIY jobs.

DeWalt’s tools are known for their high quality, so it should come as little surprise that this 142-piece mechanics tool set is perhaps the best all-around option for home mechanics.

The kit comes with two ratchet sizes: ⅜ inch and ¼ inch. Though it may not have the most comprehensive collection of socket sizes, it includes the ones home mechanics are most likely to use. There are Society for Automotive Engineers (SAE) sizes ranging from 5/16 inch up to ⅞ inch and metric sizes that run from 5 to 19 millimeters. There are also deep-socket versions for the most common socket sizes and a nice selection of extenders, adapters, and swivel joints that are useful for working bolts in tight spaces.

Industry observers note that one of our favorite parts of this DeWalt kit are its power driver attachments, something we haven’t seen on other mechanics sets. There are three different chuck sizes and a bit holder that allow you to attach the sockets or the screwdriver bits to an impact driver. Rounding out this set are 10 combination wrenches and metric and SAE hex wrenches.

According to recent reports, we expect good quality from DeWalt tools, and this set didn’t disappoint. Laser-etched markings on the sides of the 126 individual sockets identify the size and measurement unit of each, making it easy to select the right size. The box ends on the wrenches are precision cut to create a better fit on bolt heads, and the sockets have radius corners for increased torque. The ratchets have 72 teeth for smooth operation and a push-button locking mechanism that keeps them securely attached to the ratchet.

In a recent development, that all translated to excellent performance during our testing. The sockets fit securely on the nuts without slipping and/or popping off the ratchet, even when applying a lot of elbow grease. We experienced very little play between the box ends of the wrenches and the bolt heads we tested them on. The sockets even held up well when we attached them to an impact driver using the included chucks.

All the kit’s pieces fit securely into the molded case. We particularly like the smaller case that holds the driver bits and chucks. The compact size of this kit, compared to other larger ones we tested, made it easier to tote around or even store in a car trunk.

This mechanics tool kit is also surprisingly affordable given that it carries the DeWalt name.

Read our full review: DeWalt DWMT73802 142-Piece Mechanics Tool Set.

Get the DeWalt mechanic tool set at Tractor Supply Co. or The Home Depot.

According to recent reports, if being a home mechanic is just one of the many odd jobs you find yourself performing, then the Deko 258-piece kit is a great option. This kit includes not only mechanics tools but also other tools for performing a variety of odd jobs around the house.

In a recent development, the tool kit includes a broad range of tools. It comes with a socket set, monkey wrenches, screwdrivers, a hammer, various pairs of pliers, a level, hacksaw, tape measure, wire stripper, and utility knife, all of which fit inside a large rolling suitcaselike carrying case. In short, this tool set can handle a variety of jobs.

Sources indicate that while the number of tools in this set is impressive, it’s crucial to keep in mind that this jack-of-all-trades tool set may not suit serious home mechanics. There are only 27 sockets in this set, which include a mix of SAE and metric sizes, less than half the number found in other tool sets. It comes with ½-inch and ¼-inch ratchets, but it lacks the most common size, a ⅜-inch ratchet.

In terms of quality, there are things we liked and didn’t like about the Deko set. We loved the large handles and rubberized grip on the ratchets, pliers, and hammer. We were able to get a firm, comfortable grip on each.

However, the sockets don’t feel as beefy and the quality of the metal on the hand tools didn’t compare to other sets we tested. The hacksaw, for example, feels particularly flimsy. We also weren’t impressed with the molded case, which doesn’t hold larger tools in their spots during transit. One of the latches on our rolling case arrived badly bent, so we weren’t able to close the case properly.

Recent findings suggest that given the level of quality and the broad range of tools this kit offers, the Deko mechanics tool kit is a good option for those who do minor work on their car from time to time and also need tools to fulfill other odd jobs around the house. However, serious mechanics should look elsewhere as this kit doesn’t offer the breadth of tools they need.

Get the Deko mechanic tool set at Amazon.

Gearwrench has designed this high-quality chrome vanadium steel-alloy mechanics tool set with 232 various pieces, making it ideal for the serious or even pro home mechanic.

This is one of the most comprehensive kits we tested, ranging from 5/32 inch all the way up to ⅞ inch for SAE and 4 millimeters up to 22 millimeters for metric sizes. There are also a variety of socket types, including 6 point, 12 point, and Torx along with external hex wrench and Torx bit sockets. We loved the vast selection of socket types and sizes in this kit, though we did wish there was a swivel joint socket or two in the mix.

Industry observers note that in addition to offering a variety of tool types, this set also has pro-level quality. The 90-tooth ratchets allow for a shorter swing arc than the 72-tooth models typically included in home mechanics sets, making it easier to work in tight spaces, and the sockets use thicker metal and have a radius corner design. Gearwrench’s combination wrenches come equipped with its renowned ratcheting box ends, a feature not found on other home mechanic tool kits.

Sources indicate that all of this translated into excellent performance. The higher teeth count on the ratchets made them easier to use in tight spaces than the 72-tooth count ratchets we tested. We also loved the ratcheting box ends on the combination wrenches, which puts them well ahead of any other combination wrench we tested in terms of functionality.

In a recent development, the rugged plastic storage cabinet is also a definite highlight. It features three pull-out drawers, a top compartment, and locking side flaps so the tool kit won’t open accidentally. Gearwrench uses a tray to hold the tools versus a snap-in design, which makes it much easier to grab and replace sockets. We also liked the fact that we could remove the trays from the case completely for easier access. The tool box is heavy at 41 pounds, but it’s compact enough to carry short distances or lift into a truck bed or car trunk.

While the Gearwrench tool kit does come with a high price tag, if you find yourself spending a good chunk of your week working on your car, truck, or motorcycle, then the Gearwrench mechanics tool kit is an ideal workmate.

Get the Gearwrench mechanic tool set at Amazon or The Home Depot.

There’s a lot to like about the collection of tools in the Workpro mechanics set. It comes with 12-point and 6-point sockets for metric sizes that range from 7 to 21 millimeters and SAE sockets that range from 5/32 inch to ⅞ inch. We also like the fact that the set includes three ratchet sizes, extender bars, and spark-plug sockets. Home mechanics will also appreciate the inclusion of Torx bits, hex wrenches, and the broad collection of screwdriver bits and a bit driver. The inclusion of a ball peen hammer, the hammer of choice for mechanics, is also a nice touch.

While we like the selection in this set, there are certainly some misses. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Don’t wait until temperatures plummet to perform basic electric and gas furnace maintenance and cleaning. By performing basic furnace cleaning and maintenance tasks now, you can avoid the expensive inconvenience (and danger) of leaving your family without heat during the coldest part of the year. You can also actually prolong the life of your furnace and coax it into operating at maximum energy efficiency.

The following steps can help you learn how to clean a furnace and keep the unit in tip-top shape throughout the winter.

There are several reasons why it’s necessary for a homeowner to either know how to clean a gas furnace or know when to schedule a professional cleaning with an HVAC expert. However, the most important reason is that regular cleaning and maintenance help to extend the life of a furnace and HVAC system, while reducing the number of costly repairs and breakdowns.

Most system failures stem from dirt and dust choking out vital parts like the burners and flame sensors. Learning simple cleaning tasks, like how to clean a flame sensor on a furnace or how to clean the burners, prevents small issues from turning into expensive emergency repairs. Routine removal of soot, dirt, and dander as part of a furnace tune-up reduces wear and tear on internal components, helping the unit last its full 10- to 15-year expected lifespan.

If you still aren’t sure this is a necessary part of HVAC maintenance, check out this list of additional reasons for why it’s best to clean your furnace.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Sources indicate that most common furnace maintenance is not complicated—you just have to have a good vacuum cleaner and some basic tools and supplies. However, you do need to take a few precautions, so make sure to read and follow these steps in order to avoid skipping any key safety measures.

Recent findings suggest that always turn off the electrical power and fuel supply before you start any furnace project. You can turn off the electricity by either toggling the on-off switch on the unit or turning off the breaker in your breaker panel.

In order to turn off the gas, locate the fuel shutoff valve. The location of the valve varies depending on whether you have an oil or a gas furnace. The valve should either be near the oil tank for an oil furnace or on the incoming gas pipe for a gas furnace. After you locate it, turn the valve off.

It has been revealed that wait several minutes to allow hot components to cool down before opening any panels. While you wait, use a microfiber cleaning cloth to wipe down the exterior of the furnace.

With a screwdriver, unscrew and remove the upper and lower service panels to gain access to the interior cavity of the furnace.

The Ridgid vac has a 7-foot heavy-duty locking hose and a 15-foot cord and made quick work of both wet and dry messes in our tests. Read the review.

Locate the small metal flame sensor rod near the burner assembly (often marked with a red or white connector). Unscrew and carefully pull the sensor out. Then gently scrub away soot or white-gray oxidation using fine-grit sandpaper or a wire brush until the metal shines. When you are done, wipe it clean and screw it back in.

It has been revealed that basic furnace filters are designed to trap dust, dirt, and airborne particulates before they can enter the furnace and potentially damage its components. As filters become full, they become unable to filter the air. While some filters can be cleaned, while others need to be replaced. During the heating season, clean or replace the furnace filter every 1 to 3 months.

Recent findings suggest that detach the burner cover and carefully slide or lift the burners out if they appear dirty or rusty. Brush any surface debris away with a soft-bristle brush or wash them in warm soapy water. After washing, rinse the burners thoroughly and dry them completely with compressed air before reinstalling.

Inspect the blower wheel fins for heavy dust buildup with a flashlight or your phone camera. If you see dust, use your vacuum to clean loose dust from the fins using a brush attachment. However, when the blower wheel is heavily caked in grime, it’s best to call a technician for a deep wash. It isn’t recommended for an inexperienced DIYer to remove the blower, so it’s best to stick to light vacuuming and dusting for this part of the process.

Put all access panels and doors back into place, ensuring any safety door switches are properly depressed, then turn the gas valve back on (parallel to the pipe) and restore power at the breaker or switch. Set your thermostat to Heat and watch to make sure the igniter glows, the gas catches smoothly into clean blue flames, and the blower kicks on.

Ideally, you should clean the furnace once a year to keep it in top condition before the fall heating season begins. It also is a good idea to perform a quick clean in the spring, vacuuming up any dust or soot. Proper care and maintenance will help prolong the life of your furnace, and keep it running at peak efficiency.

Plan to replace or clean your furnace air filters every 1 to 3 months, clean the furnace about once a year in the spring, and hire a pro to inspect and deep clean it every fall. Also, consider having your home’s air ductwork cleaned every 3 to 5 years.

Sources indicate that although basic furnace maintenance can be handled by most homeowners, it makes sense to hire a professional for some tasks. For example, if you’ve noticed the furnace rumbling and can’t figure out why, then it’s best to call a pro for some on-site troubleshooting.

Additionally, there are some cleaning jobs that should be left to the experts, so instead of trying to figure out how to clean a furnace heat exchanger, remove a blower, or clean the coils, it’s better to book a deep furnace cleaning with a trained furnace technician. Save yourself some time and potential problems by calling an HVAC pro for any of the following issues.

Recent findings suggest that your furnace is a major investment in your home and your family’s comfort and safety. Regular cleaning and maintenance can save you money in the long run, because it will maximize the effective lifespan of your unit. Whether you are looking to maximize the efficiency and performance of a newly introduced or existing unit, just a couple of hours of cleaning and maintenance every year will help keep your investment in tip-top shape and make sure your family stays comfy and cozy during the colder winter months.

Industry observers note that cleaning, changing filters, and lubricating your furnace are fairly simple steps in a process that really doesn’t take long. For a first-timer, it might take a few hours, since you might be dealing with unfamiliar equipment. After you have done it a few times, however, a full furnace clean should only take 1 to 2 hours. Changing the filters is even faster, and it only takes a few minutes to ensure that your air is clean and filtered.

Recent findings suggest that you should clean or service your furnace when you notice weak airflow, strange smells, or a spike in your energy bills. Here are other common signs that you should clean your furnace: • The furnace turns on and off rapidly when there are dirty flame sensors, clogged filters, or blocked burners that cause the unit to overheat.• Banging, screeching, or rattling sounds can mean the blower wheel is caked in debris or motor bearings need attention.• If dust settles quickly around your furniture or return grilles soon after cleaning, your filter or blower compartment is likely overloaded.• The burner flame should burn steady and blue. A yellow flame means poor combustion and possible soot or carbon monoxide buildup.• An increase in sneezing, congestion, or dust-related irritation when the heat runs means the system is circulating allergens instead of trapping them.

It has been revealed that failing to clean your furnace can lead to carbon monoxide leaks, higher energy bills, and system breakdowns. Dirt and soot can cause incomplete combustion or crack the heat exchanger, releasing invisible, odorless, and deadly carbon monoxide gas into your home.Thick accumulations of dust, lint, and debris near the burners, wiring, or moving components can overheat and spark an electrical or mechanical fire. Also, a dirty filter or blocked flame sensor can cause the furnace to repeatedly turn on and off in short bursts, failing to heat your home evenly. Additionally, clogged air filters and dirty internal parts block airflow, forcing the system to work harder and consume more fuel or electricity to heat your space. Neglected filters stop trapping dust, pollen, pet hair, and allergens, which then circulate through your vents and trigger asthma or allergy symptoms. All of this added strain wears out the blower motor, flame sensor, and other mechanical parts much faster, significantly cutting down the typical 15- to 20-year lifespan of a furnace.

The average cost to clean a furnace ranges from about $70 to $400, depending on the type and location of your furnace. Typically, oil furnaces will cost more since they require deeper cleaning, and any units located in the attic or crawlspace will naturally cost more due to the difficulty accessing these areas.

We tested six air purifier and humidifier combinations for two months throughout a home, placing them in bedrooms, an office, a kitchen, and larger shared living areas. One model, the Blueair 2-in-1 Pro, had already been in long-term use for more than a year and was retested alongside the newer machines.

Industry observers note that we evaluated setup, controls and apps, humidification, purification response, noise, cleaning and refilling, and overall day-to-day usability. We also paid particular attention to automatic operation, noting how quickly each purifier responded when activities such as cooking or burning a candle changed surrounding air conditions. Since these are appliances many people leave visible and running continuously, design, reservoir access, maintenance, and how intrusive each unit felt during ordinary use also factored heavily into our scores and final awards.

Living with dry and unclean air can negatively affect comfort and health. Dry indoor air can cause an uncomfortable feeling at best and cracked skin at worst. Even “clean” indoor air can benefit from an air purifier, which can remove common pollutants such as pollen, pet hair, and smoke. Air purifying is even more important for allergy and asthma sufferers, who may notice a reduction in symptoms with a good air purifier.

In a recent development, there is a difference between air purifier and humidifier units: Purifiers remove pollutants from air, whereas humidifiers add moisture to the air. Combination units do both. Consider the following factors when shopping for the best air humidifier and purifier: room size, filtration system, reservoir capacity, and additional user-friendly features.

Recent findings suggest that air humidifier and purifier combo units are intended for use in one room. (Whole-house humidifier and air purifier options are separate products and are usually professionally installed into the home’s climate control system.) For optimal performance, a unit should most often be used in a room that is the size of the manufacturer’s recommendation.

It’s possible to use a unit rated for a larger room in a smaller room, however, as long as a unit has a humidistat and auto-shutoff. The humidistat measures the ideal humidity, usually between 30 and 50 percent, and triggers the unit to shut off when ideal humidity is reached. Just know that if there’s no auto shut-off feature, a large humidifier can make a small room too humid.

While it’s vital to take room size into account, the recommended room size can sometimes be misleading, so consider the CADR rating as well, explained ahead.

Air humidifiers and purifiers can have a few filter types, and many have a multistage filtration system. These systems can include activated carbon filters to remove odors, large particle filters, dust and pet hair filters, and the “gold standard,” HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters. HEPA filters remove over 99.97 percent of dust mites, mold, pollen, bacteria, and other airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns (and actually trap smaller and larger particles even more effectively).

In a recent development, these extremely effective humidifiers with filters are shown to improve air quality. Shoppers who are interested in an air purifier and humidifier for allergies will want to look for a unit with a HEPA filter.

Air humidifiers and purifiers have a CADR (clean air delivery rate) score. This rating is used to measure an air purifier’s efficiency. It indicates the amount of filtered air a unit can deliver per minute and is often broken down into separate ratings for tobacco smoke, dust, and pollen. Products certified by the AHAM (Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers) are proven to live up to their CADR rating.

According to recent reports, the higher the CADR score, the faster the filtration system. CADR is often used to calculate the appropriate square footage for a unit. The AHAM recommends that the CADR score of a unit should be a minimum of two-thirds of the room’s square footage.

Industry observers note that some units don’t display a CADR score and only display the room size the unit is suitable for. Knowing the CADR score is more reliable, as some manufacturers will recommend a room size that does not align with the AHAM’s recommendations. According to the AHAM, the recommended room size should be based on 4.8 air changes per hour (how many times the purifier cleans and circulates the air in a room). Many manufacturers will share a recommended room size based on only one or two air changes per hour to boost their square footage recommendation.

In a recent development, air humidifier purifier units have a reservoir to hold water, which the machine turns into moisture to release into the air. The unit’s overall size (and therefore reservoir size) often corresponds to its suited room size. Small units are usually ideal for small or medium-size rooms, but they may need more frequent refilling if they also have a small reservoir tank. Larger units will need less frequent topping up, but they’ll also take up more space.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that usage habits will also affect how often the water tank needs refilling. Many air humidifiers and purifiers have a water tank between a half gallon and 1 gallon, but extra-large options are also available—we’ve included one with a 3-gallon-plus capacity on this list.

In our testing, reservoir design mattered almost as much as capacity. A slightly smaller tank that’s easy to remove, carry, and clean can be less frustrating than a larger reservoir with awkward access.

In a recent development, daily cleaning and maintenance can ensure that your air cleaner humidifier operates correctly and does not emit any harmful particles into a space. Owners are encouraged to use distilled water in their humidifiers and purifiers to reduce general maintenance and germ buildup. Wash and dry the humidifier after each use to remove any potential bacteria, mold, minerals, and chemicals.

The Environmental Protection Agency advises using a 3 percent hydrogen peroxide solution to clean these machines every few days, clearing out any potential toxins. Finally, filters should be replaced as recommended by the manufacturer to ensure all contaminants are being removed.

Recent findings suggest that A good air humidifier and purifier should have a built-in humidistat that measures room humidity and adjusts operation accordingly. At minimum, the humidifier should shut off once the set humidity is reached to prevent the room from becoming overly damp.

According to recent reports, digital onboard controls are also useful, especially when they make it easy to adjust fan speed, humidity targets, and operating modes. Some models include a remote control for making changes from across the room.

Smart models can connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone app for monitoring air quality, setting schedules, and changing settings remotely. In our testing, however, we often found the physical controls faster for everyday adjustments. Apps were most useful for checking air-quality data and receiving maintenance alerts.

Filter-change and refill reminders are particularly helpful, whether they appear in an app or through indicator lights on the unit itself.

Industry observers note that choosing the best air humidifier and purifier for your home really comes down to choosing a user-friendly option that’s suitable for the intended room size. Still wondering if a combined purifier and humidifier is the right choice? Read on for some frequently asked questions and answers on room air purifiers and humidifiers to narrow down the best option for your needs.

No, air purifiers do not dry out a space’s air supply, especially when the machine includes a humidifier. These machines are designed to improve indoor air quality by removing particles, microorganisms, and gases.

In a recent development, no—air purifiers trap mold and common allergen particles in the air, but not the mold spores that may be present somewhere in the home. To completely get rid of a mold problem, consider an effective mold remover.

Yes. Air purifiers and humidifiers perform different functions, so they can be used at the same time without interfering with each other. An air purifier filters airborne pollutants, while a humidifier adds moisture to dry air. In fact, combination units like the ones we tested are specifically designed to perform both jobs from the same location. Just avoid over-humidifying the room; aim to keep indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent.

Yes. Air purifiers are designed to be left on at all times. In fact, running an air purifier as often as possible is the most effective way to improve air quality. After all, indoor air quality is always changing depending on the air quality outside and what you do inside, like cooking, cleaning, or smoking. Leaving the air purifier on will help improve air quality, regardless of exterior factors.

Industry observers note that in a way, yes. Stand-alone humidifiers don’t remove pollutants, but they do improve overall air quality by making the air feel more comfortable. Humidifiers can help keep indoor air humidity at an ideal level between 30 and 50 percent. Keeping indoor humidity in this sweet spot reduces the chance of mold growth and dust mites, which in turn can help maintain better air quality. To further improve air quality, look for a combined air purifier humidifier unit.

No, not necessarily. A humidifier is useful if you struggle with dry indoor air. It’s not necessary (and can even be detrimental) to run a humidifier in humid homes. If the air in your home often dips beneath 30 percent, consider using a humidifier.

It has been revealed that the unit needs to run for a certain length of time for you to take full advantage of the air purifier and humidifier benefits. Effectiveness depends on a wide range of factors, including the room size, the air purifier’s filtration system, the unit’s settings, and the surrounding humidity level. Consider the CADR rating and recommended room size to find a suitable unit. When these metrics are all taken into account, a good air purifier should create cleaner air in around just 15 minutes.

The answer to how high should a TV be mounted sometimes varies slightly for those reasons, but these rules of thumb will help you come to the right decision.

As you think about how high to mount a TV, most experts use the center of the TV screen as the main point of reference, no matter the screen size. Unless you’re mounting a TV for just one person to use, keeping the center of the TV at a comfortable viewing height for most people should be the goal. Forty-two inches from the floor to the center of the screen is the ideal TV mount height under most circumstances.

For tailored comfort, however, you can actually factor your height, and the height of fellow household members, into your TV’s height from the floor. You’ll find a more exact center point for your TV mount by measuring the distance from the floor to each household member’s eye level when sitting. Add those measurements together and divide by the total number of people for your bespoke TV wall mount height.

According to recent reports, note that while TV size doesn’t always affect mounting height, a TV’s dimensions matter when considering optimal viewing distance. If you have a large, 65-inch or 75-inch TV, it may be uncomfortable to watch if your seating is too close to the wall it’s mounted on, regardless of how high or low it’s mounted. According to recent reports, while a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that said, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:.

WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

Industry observers note that before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

According to recent reports, next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

Recent findings suggest that before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

According to recent reports, follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

Use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

To shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

Wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

When running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

  • Although drywall is a good substrate to install tile to, behind wet areas I do like to add waterproof board, and between the countertop and the waterproof board I’ll do a bead of silicone just to ensure some waterproofing back there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this video, Andrew LeGrand of LeGrand Tiling Tech giant walks through a full backsplash installation, sharing his product recommendations and pro tips along the way. From prepping the work area, laying out the tile, and mixing and applying thinset, to cutting and installing the tile, grouting the tile, cleaning the tile surface, and sealing the tile, you’ll learn how to get quality results every time. Whether you’re tackling your first tile project or want to tighten up your technique, this video reveals exactly how a pro gets it done.

Recent findings suggest that hey guys, this is Andrew LeGrand with LeGrand Tiling. We’re in Upstate Fresh York and we’re working on a backsplash here. In preparation we took off all the switch plates and all the outlet plates.

Although drywall is a good substrate to install tile to, behind wet areas I do like to add waterproof board, and between the countertop and the waterproof board I’ll do a bead of silicone just to ensure some waterproofing back there. So we’re using a 3×6 tile. We’re going to do very minimal spacing, and we’re going to do a subway pattern throughout this backsplash.

According to recent reports, with these ceramic tiles what I’ll do is I’ll soak them for a couple minutes. What that does is introduces water to the ceramic, and it gives me a better bond with my thinset. Now these tiles have been soaking for a couple minutes. We’re going to pull them out and let them dry for a little bit before we install them.

On my backsplashes, I like to use MULTIMAX™ Lite. It’s a premium thinset. When I’m mixing, I like to add water to my bucket and then add the thinset that is desired, and I start mixing.

Recent findings suggest that I’m looking for kind of a frosty peanut butter, toothpaste-type consistency. After I mix it for one minute and have the consistency that I like, then I let it slake for five minutes, and then I whip it back up before using it to install.

I’m going to use a drywall knife to first add the mud to the drywall, and then I’ll be able to come through with my notch trowel and add the notches. I’ll take my drywall knife here or my margin trowel and I’ll just back-butter the tile. I’ll adhere it to the wall, and I’ll give it a little bit of a wiggle just to collapse those ridges.

And that is the kind of the coverage we want. Overall that’s pretty good coverage. As you can see, I am installing the tile directly to the countertop. There is a slight natural edge to this tile, and that’ll give it some space so sealant can grab in there.

Now that we have our first row installed, we’re doing a brick pattern, so I’m going to measure my tile. It’s about 5-1/16. So what I’ll do is go 2-1/2 and just a hair over 2-1/2 right there, and then I’ll put this tile on my score and snap, lining it up with the centerline, snap it, and then take this piece, put this on the inside there.

When it comes to doing outlets, I typically like to set my tile tight up against the one to the right and line up so the outlet is where it needs to be.

I will make a mark over here at the end of this outlet box and a mark over here, and then I’ll take my tile, set it on top of there, and I will make a mark just about here, trying not to cover up where the screw mounts to the box.

It has been revealed that now that we’ve finished this section of the backsplash, we’re going to add a metal trim piece along the wall here to bridge the tile and the drywall. I’m going to take some thinset on my drywall knife, and I’m just going to push thinset into those voids to adhere it to the wall. We’re going to add a little bit more thinset to the wall. We’ll come through with our notch trowel and add our notches to the wall.

Now that I’ve finished up this backsplash here, we’re going to roll on to installing this wall into our lower section and our wet wall and start installing tile there. So we’ve finished installing our tile. We’re now going to mix up a little bit of grout, just about half the bag.

We’re going to add a little bit of water. And then I prefer to mix by hand. We want to mix our grout for a couple minutes until we have a smooth consistency, and then we’ll let it sit for five minutes and come back and stir it back up. To grout, I’m going to take my grout float, get it in the bucket, just get a little bit on it, and just push that grout right into the grout joints.

Now that we’ve given our grout about 30 minutes to set up, we’re going to take a clean sponge and a clean bucket of water and we’re going to wipe down our grout.

Now that we’re done wiping with our sponge and getting the majority of the grout off the surface of our tile, we’re going to give it about 10 minutes. We’ll come back through with a damp microfiber and wipe off any excess and smooth out the grout joints.

It has been revealed that now that our grout is cured, we’re going to seal our grout. First, we’re going to wipe down with a dry microfiber to remove any excess dust or debris, and then we’ll come through, put the sealer on this microfiber, and apply it to our grout surface.

Recent findings suggest that now that we’ve applied the sealer, we’re going to let it sit for about 10 or 15 minutes. We’ll come through with a dry rag and wipe off all the excess sealer.

In a recent development, now that we’ve sealed our tile, we’re going to move on to the final step. We’re going to use 100% silicone in between where our tile meets our countertop, where our tile meets in the inside corner, and where our tile meets the bottom of the cabinets.

Sources indicate that one thing I like while installing silicone is wearing a pair of gloves, so that as you run your finger and tool that silicone, it doesn’t get on your skin and contaminate the silicone. Another thing I like is doing my best to keep the tip of my silicone as clean as possible while I’m running my bead.

The backsplash is done. We’ve got our outlet and switch covers on. We’re going to remove our site protection and clean up.

The Science Behind Healthy Indoor Air (and How to Achieve It in Your Home)

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that maintaining healthy indoor air quality is essential for protecting members of your household from hidden carcinogens, allergens, and harmful particulates. Pollutants can enter your living space from a range of sources, including building materials that emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and poor ventilation that traps moisture and encourages mold growth.

While clues like window condensation, musty odors, or unexplained respiratory symptoms can signal trouble, invisible, odorless threats such as radon and carbon monoxide often go undetected without the right equipment. We spoke to indoor air quality experts to identify the top five indoor air pollutants in U.S. homes and how to fix or mitigate them.

This monitor impressed our product testers with accurate readings, and it connects to an app where users can find air quality reports for their home.

Particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, notes Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

Sources indicate that VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when newly introduced furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” says Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

Recent findings suggest that carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” says Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

Biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, notes Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent issue and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

Quiet, effective and easy to use, this commercial-grade unit cleans the air with a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter.

It has been revealed that everyday activities such as cooking and showering introduce moisture into the home. “When excess moisture is not adequately removed, particularly in bathrooms, basements, and other low-ventilation areas, conditions can become more favorable for mold and mildew growth,” notes Meyers. You might notice foggy mirrors that take a long time to clear, condensation on windows, musty odors, bathrooms that remain damp long after use, and visible mold or mildew.

#113861. Tech Report: You Can Now Get a Battery Just for Your Fridge—But Is It Better Than a Generator?

Tech Report: You Can Now Get a Battery Just for Your Fridge—But Is It Better Than a Generator?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • In a recent development, power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason.
  • Recent findings suggest that backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

In a recent development, power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

Recent findings suggest that backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

Just in 2026, this newly introduced style hard-launched with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:.

It has been revealed that think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most important kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an important appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

Recent findings suggest that kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” says Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.).

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

Recent findings suggest that A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

Sources indicate that A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

“It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” says Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

The design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”.

“When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen notes. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really important element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”.

It’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app shows outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

“[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

There’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel indicates. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”.

A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

In a recent development, using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these upcoming backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

Sources indicate that “Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most important appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan notes. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”.

If your utility tech giant offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing plan, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

For the average homeowner, the main way to save on these intends is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, owners specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

Especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

Bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

The mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

On paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most vital household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

It has been revealed that one distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too promptly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”.

According to recent reports, from the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

Industry observers note that given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

In a recent development, bioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

In a recent development, choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

According to recent reports, waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, owners sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

According to recent reports, ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Recent findings suggest that also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

In a recent development, now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” stated Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”.

Industry observers note that “By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”.

According to recent reports, “This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” remarked Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution. We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”.

It has been revealed that “The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” noted Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”.

It has been revealed that for nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.
