To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

Industry observers note that after selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

Industry observers note that the best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

Recent findings suggest that countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

Reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Significant Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

It has been revealed that countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

In a recent development, two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more crucial to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

It has been revealed that most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Recent findings suggest that reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

Many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

Then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

Industry observers note that capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

Flow rate—how promptly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another crucial consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

Every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

Industry observers note that A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

According to recent reports, water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

Recent findings suggest that no, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

It has been revealed that most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need upcoming filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

In a recent development, victory! Millions of Americans want and need low-FODMAP foods, which are low in certain sugars that can cause debilitating stomach problems, aggravate irritable bowels, and worse. Fortunately, this week (following the Ninth Circuit's revival of our First Amendment challenge), the FDA lifted its ban on producers truthfully labelling their products "Low-FODMAP." States IJ client Michelle Przybocki, who abides by a strict low-FODMAP diet after nearly dying from digestive complications, "I'm thrilled that the federal government is going to allow companies to start labeling their products as 'Low-FODMAP,' because this makes it easier for me to find foods that I know will not cause me digestive issues." Click here to learn more.

In a recent development, new on the Short Circuit podcast: Fancy some Elevenses? Serving up Eleventh Circuit refreshments in our #12Months12Circuits series. There's excessive bail in Alabama and excessive bar fees in Florida.

According to recent reports, friends, if a federal official violates your constitutional rights, your options for being made whole by money damages have been all but extinguished in recent years, leaving the feds with something akin to absolute immunity for all kinds of misconduct and misdeeds. But there has to be some avenue for accountability. So here at IJ, we're pushing back, not only on the late-lamented Bivens cause of action, but also on the too-narrowly construed Federal Tort Claims Act. And then, of course, there's the traditional source of accountability that the Founders would have recognized (and that the Supreme Court's Bivens skeptics preferred): state law causes of action, like California's traditional tort system and the state's Bane Act. All of which were on the table at oral argument in the Ninth Circuit this week, where we're happy to report we had an engaged, cross-ideological panel. Click here to learn more.

I’ve tested a lot of air purifiers, and most look like appliances I’d rather tuck out of sight in a corner. The Dupray Bloom Air Purifier is different. It combines a HEPA air purifier with a removable planter, turning something purely functional into a decorative accent. I planted a small fiddle-leaf fig in mine, and I love how it looks in the room. But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

Sources indicate that absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

It has been revealed that there is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

In a recent development, I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

Sources indicate that behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

Industry observers note that one feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

Sources indicate that the Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

According to recent reports, it’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

Another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

My only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a upcoming prescription for glasses.

At $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

Dupray advertises coverage up to 1,517 square feet, but that’s based on just one air change per hour. For more frequent air cleaning, it’s rated to cover 316 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. I’d use that smaller figure when choosing where to place it.

The Bloom also offers an optional wood tabletop model for anyone who prefers an accent table instead of a planter.

I love having a living plant incorporated into an appliance I’d otherwise try to hide. The Bloom is one of the few air purifiers I’ve tested that I’d happily put on display.

Latest Update: Gun Rights and Guilt by Association

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v.
  • Industry observers note that the San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club….
  • Recent findings suggest that kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v. County of San Diego, decided today by Ninth Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, joined by Judges Kenneth Lee and Jennifer Sung:.

Industry observers note that the San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club…. [We conclude, among other things, that] the district court improperly dismissed his First Amendment [freedom of association] claim….

Recent findings suggest that kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California. He's a member of the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which, according to Shilling, was founded in 1946 by World War II veterans. In his view, it's not like some other motorcycle clubs, which are known for criminal and gang activity. Instead, the Boozefighters focus on charitable work and the "core values of family, work, and community." Shilling's record is clean; he has no criminal history.

It has been revealed that in June 2022, when the "good moral character" requirement [for getting a concealed carry license] still existed [under California law], Shilling applied for and received a CCW license from then-San Diego County Sheriff Anthony Ray. This was short lived. Less than a year and a half later, in December 2023, a different San Diego County Sheriff, Kelly Martinez, used the "good moral character" requirement to revoke Shilling's CCW license. In a letter notifying Shilling of the revocation, Sheriff Martinez explained that the "San Diego Sheriff's Department['s] good moral character definition" excludes a person who:.

In a recent development, has a pattern of or propensity for criminal conduct, as demonstrated by anything in the application or investigation for a license. This includes, but is not limited to, evidence of criminal behavior or a close nexus to a criminal gang. In making this determination, the Sheriff's Department shall use an objective inquiry, considering the facts and circumstances known at the time of the application or through the investigation.

The letter remarked that Shilling's license was revoked due to his association with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which the Sheriff described as a "criminal street gang." Shilling was not given the opportunity to contest the allegations before his license was revoked, but he could request reconsideration of the decision. The new CCW regime with the "dangerousness" requirement took effect on January 1, 2024, shortly after Shilling's license was revoked….

Here's the court's analysis allowing Shilling's First Amendment freedom of association claim to go forward:.

The First Amendment guarantees all Americans the "right to associate with others." … [T]he right protects groups of individuals "in pursuit of a wide variety of political, social, economic, educational, religious and cultural ends." ….

The government may infringe the freedom of association in "varied ways," including by "punish[ing] individuals for their affiliations." The government cannot impose "criminal sanctions or deny[ ] rights and privileges solely because of a citizen's association with an unpopular organization." For example, a group of students could not be denied the "benefits" of official campus recognition at a state college merely because of its affiliation with a national organization associated with disruptive and violent campus activity…. [Likewise,] "Civil liability may not be imposed merely because an individual belonged to a group, some members of which committed acts of violence." … If the government seeks to deprive an individual of a benefit, privilege, or right based on association with an alleged criminal organization, "it is necessary to establish that the group itself possessed unlawful goals and that the individual held a specific intent to further those illegal aims." ….

Given this understanding of the First Amendment, Shilling easily pleaded a violation of his freedom of association…. [His] allegations sufficiently raise an infringement of Shilling's free-association right because the Sheriff deprived him of a benefit, privilege, or right—the ability to carry a concealed weapon in public—"solely because of [his] association with an unpopular organization." Unless the Sheriff adequately meets her burden of showing the Boozefighters "possessed unlawful goals" and Shilling's "specific intent to further those illegal aims," she cannot "punish [Shilling] for [his] affiliations." This kind of "guilt by association alone, without establishing that an individual's association poses the threat feared by the Government, is an impermissible basis upon which to deny First Amendment rights.".

In dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free-association right. It asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the Club's activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a group's lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, it's infringed in "varied ways." And "denying" an individual benefits, rights, or privileges "solely because of [his] association"—as Shilling alleges—is certainly another way….

For the court's analysis of sovereign immunity and of whether Schilling's Second Amendment claim was moot, see the full opinion.

Gary W. Gorski (Veterans Law Center) represents plaintiff.

Recent findings suggest that at $2,395 for the king size I tested, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper is absolutely a luxury purchase. After sleeping on it for 2 months during a Florida summer, however, I can say that its temperature-control technology delivers. This 2-inch topper uses fans, airflow, heating elements, and temperature sensors to regulate each side of the bed independently, creating a surprisingly effective way to stay comfortable throughout the night. While some aspects of the design could use a little more refinement, the actual cooling performance left me impressed.

Installation was straightforward. I unpacked the vacuum-sealed topper, laid it over my king mattress, added my usual fitted sheet, and plugged it in. The power supply is fairly big, but I had no trouble tucking it down behind my headboard. The cables emerge from the head of the topper, which is worth keeping in mind if you tend to stretch your arms overhead while sleeping. As for comfort, the topper has an unusual feel at first—slightly firm but with enough give to stay comfortable. Its internal mesh structure allows air to circulate beneath you, and the effect is immediately noticeable, even on lower settings.

The cooling performance is easily my favorite feature. Even at level 3, I could feel a gentle, pleasant stream of cool air underneath me, which was especially welcome during warm Florida nights. The one trade-off is fan noise, which becomes quite noticeable at higher settings. Anything above level 5 was too loud for my sleeping preferences, but I found an easy workaround using the app’s scheduling feature. I’d run the cooling at a higher setting for about an hour before bedtime, then lower it to level 3 when I climbed into bed. This gave me the best of both worlds: a wonderfully cool mattress at bedtime and gentle, nearly silent cooling throughout the night.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few areas where I’d love to see Perfectly Snug make improvements, especially considering the premium price. The power supply and small side-mounted control panel are functional but have a fairly basic appearance. I also occasionally brushed against the fans positioned at the foot of the topper, which could briefly interrupt their operation (making a noticeable “you’ve just stopped a fan from moving” type of buzzing sound). The companion app was another underwhelming aspect of the experience. While it offers useful features like scheduling and temperature adjustments, its interface feels super dated and could benefit from a much more polished, intuitive design. None of these issues prevented me from enjoying the topper, but they’re details I’d expect to see addressed at this price point.

Ultimately, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper gets the most notable thing right: keeping your bed at a comfortable temperature. I enjoyed slipping into a perfectly cooled bed each night, and the subtle airflow on lower settings noticeably improved my sleep comfort. It’s an innovative product with plenty to offer, particularly for hot sleepers or couples with different temperature preferences. Although the fan noise and a few less-refined design elements keep it from feeling like a truly premium experience, the core technology is admirable. With some thoughtful improvements, this could be an outstanding luxury sleep upgrade.

Leaf vacuums come in various types and with different-size collection bags. There are also three power source types—gas, electric, and cordless/battery—with each option affecting runtime and suction. Take a look below at some notable factors to help determine the motor type, power, and design that will work best for you.

Leaf vacuums are made in a few types, and some kinds work better in certain situations and setups than others.

Like lawn mowers, leaf vacuums are available in electric- and gas-powered versions.

In a recent development, to figure out the power of a leaf vacuum, check the product description for two numbers: mph and CFM. The mph stands for miles per hour—in this case, referring to how quickly air is suctioned into the unit and through the tube. Most units run between 110 and 180 mph, although some may reach extremes of 250 mph or so.

In a recent development, somewhat more important than airspeed, however, is CFM. This describes how much air moves through the vacuum in the span of 60 seconds, indicating how powerful the unit is. While mph provides an idea of how rapidly leaves can go through the tube, CFM indicates how much can go through all at once.

Industry observers note that the CFM rankings for leaf vacuums range between 150 to 600. A unit with a CFM under 200 may be all that’s needed to clean up an apartment balcony or a small yard, but for larger areas, it may be desirable to invest in a unit with higher CFM.

Saunders recommends a leaf vacuum with a strong motor “that can really get the job done.” He adds, “Something like a 12-amp electric motor, which you’ll find in some top models, will give you the suction power you need to handle a good amount of leaves without getting bogged down.”.

The runtime of a battery-powered leaf vacuum can limit the amount of work that can be done. Most models offer at least 20 to 30 minutes of runtime on the highest power levels. At lower levels, the battery may run for 45 minutes or more.

It has been revealed that battery-powered models that include two or more interchangeable batteries can increase the available work time. While one battery is in use, the other battery charges. Charge times vary from 1.5 to 3 hours and sometimes longer depending on the battery size. The amount of work may still be limited with interchangeable batteries, but it will provide more work time than a single battery.

Some manufacturers provide batteries that are interchangeable with the brand’s other power tools. In these cases, buying power tools of the same brand can add to the number of batteries available. Ultimately, that can extend possible work time even more.

Some leaf vacuums offer bells and whistles beyond simple suction. In fact, most vacuums these days are actually leaf blowers with a vacuum function. That provides extra use options with a single tool.

Leaf vacuums are best suited for smaller outdoor spaces, like those surrounding garden apartments and duplexes. Some models also offer a mulching option, which is great for repurposing leaves into healthy plant beds.

A leaf vacuum’s mix of features and design can make it easier or harder to use. Bag size, for example, determines how often it will need to be emptied. Larger bags mean less frequent emptying, but they can be awkward and heavy to carry.

According to recent reports, weight also affects ease of use. Gas-powered leaf vacuums weigh the most, though some battery-powered models are almost as heavy. For those with a large yard, gas power makes sense because it can keep a consistent high power throughout the whole yard.

However, for those with smaller yards, the lightweight nature of a handheld or a battery-powered model can be more comfortable. Models with a backpack bag combine the lighter weight of a handheld leaf vacuum with the convenience of a backpack.

Sources indicate that ergonomics is also something to take into consideration. “You’re going to be using this tool for a while, so it needs to be comfortable,” Saunders states. “Lightweight models are easier on the arms and back, especially if you’re working in a large yard. Features like an ergonomically designed tube can also make a significant difference by reducing strain.”.

Industry observers note that finally, there are controls to consider. Trigger switches and on/off buttons directly on the handle are easier to use. This allows you to turn the machine on or off with one hand. Toolless conversion for hybrid models can also add to ease of use.

It has been revealed that leaf vacuums aren’t complicated once you understand how they work and what features are needed for specific jobs. However, since they aren’t as common as leaf blowers, you might still find yourself scratching your head as you look at the specs. Here, we answer some of the most common questions about leaf vacuums to help you make the right choice.

A leaf vacuum is the best machine for picking up leaves. Choose one that matches your yard size and typical leaf volume. Battery-powered handheld models work best for small yards with a moderate amount of leaves. Electric and gas models offer longer running times and a larger collection bag capacity for larger areas and heavier leaf cover.

A leaf vacuum needs a minimum rating of 340 CFM and 150 mph to pick up dry material effectively. Leaf removal equipment rated above 500 CFM and 180 mph is best for large areas and wet leaves and debris.

Yes, a lawn vacuum will effectively pick up dry and clumped grass clippings.

No, leaf vacuums are not designed to clean gutters. They don’t offer the required suction or reach to do the job.

To switch a dual-purpose leaf blower/vac from blower to vacuum mode, remove the blower tube and intake guard; then attach the vacuum tube (to the air intake) and the collection bag (where the blower tube came off). Check the owner’s manual for specific instructions.

Yes, leaf vacuums can be noisy, especially those with gas engines. Some models can reach 90 decibels. However, those powered by rechargeable batteries are much quieter, in the 60 to 80 decibel range.

Sources indicate that to clean an outdoor vacuum for leaves, first turn it off and disconnect the power cord or battery. Empty the collection bag, including anything that may not easily dump out. Remove and unclog the suction nozzle, and clear any debris from the impeller.

Leaf vacuums will last 8 to 10 years or longer with routine maintenance.

Leaf vacuum prices range from about $100 to more than $1000, depending on the design and size.

Second Amendment as a Right to Sell Guns as Well as to Have and Buy Them?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S.
  • Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C.
  • The district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S. v. Deare:.

Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a)(1) and for making false statements with respect to records of licensed firearms dealers. Deare then filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, broadly challenging the constitutionality of § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements.

The district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms. The court further held that, even if federal licensing requirements are implicated by the Second Amendment, such requirements are consistent with our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation….

Deare primarily challenges the district court's denial of his motion to dismiss the indictment. Specifically, he argues that the Second Amendment's plain text covers firearm sales, and that § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements are inconsistent with our Nation's history of firearm regulation.

The plain text of the Second Amendment covers the sale of firearms. As we noted in Reese v. BATFE (5th Cir. 2025), "the right to 'keep and bear arms' surely implies the right to purchase them." During oral argument, the government conceded that the Second Amendment applies to the commercial sale of firearms.

Accordingly, we vacate the district court's order denying Deare's motion to dismiss the indictment and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

(As I read the opinion, it doesn't affect the false statements charge.).

It's gratifying that our court today reaffirms what we should have long understood—that the Second Amendment right to "keep and bear Arms" plainly encompasses the sale of arms as well. It seems obvious that constitutional rights are meaningless if the Government can simply prohibit the means by which citizens are able to exercise those rights.

Recent findings suggest that our dissenting colleague theorizes that 18 U.S.C. § 922(a) is not about constitutional rights, but about commercial regulation. It's the same view expressed by the district court below: "§ 922(a)(1) is a modest regulation of the commercial activity of selling/transferring firearms to others…. [F]ederal licensure and record keeping requirements do not affect an individual's rights to possess firearms…. [T]hese requirements affect only the seller. As such, Defendants have failed to persuade this Court that these commercial licensure and recordkeeping requirements implicate the Second Amendment.".

Or as the dissent puts it simply, "the Second Amendment … doesn't mention sellers," so "I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered.".

By that logic, the First Amendment doesn't mention sellers, so presumably booksellers aren't covered by the First Amendment, either. But that can't be right.

Constitutional rights are constitutional rights, regardless of whether they're compensated—as I've noted on a number of occasions. And if that's true under the First Amendment, then it should be equally true in Second Amendment challenges to § 922(a) as well….

In a recent development, our dissenting colleague responds by offering a textual distinction between the First and Second Amendments. At bottom, the dissent theorizes that the "freedom of speech" contemplates sales, whereas "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms" does not. But with respect, I don't see the textual distinction that she sees. The theory is also hard to square with what we saw in Villarreal.….

Judge Oldham, joined by Judge Ho, concurred in the judgment (though presumably they also joined their own unsigned opinion):.

Industry observers note that the first question presented is whether restrictions on the sale of firearms burden the Second Amendment rights of American citizens. They do—in at least two ways. First, such restrictions directly burden the seller's right to keep and bear arms. And second, they burden the prospective buyer's right to keep and bear arms, because the right to keep an item always includes the right to acquire it.

It has been revealed that start with the constitutional text. The Second Amendment does not just prohibit the government from denying the right to keep and bear arms. Instead, it says that the right cannot be "infringed." And at the Founding, "infringe" meant "violate," "destroy," or "hinder." Thus, the government cannot hinder the people's rights to keep and bear arms.

Restrictions on sale hinder both the seller's and buyer's right to keep and bear arms. Start with the seller's right to possess firearms. The Second Amendment guarantees the right to keep guns for personal use, and the seller is an individual who can lawfully possess guns. And it's hornbook property law that the right to possess an article "includes the right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." So the right to keep a gun must include the right to dispose of that gun as the owner sees fit. This is not an independent "right to sell." Rather, my point is that governmental interference with the right to sell a firearm is itself a burden on the seller's existing property right in that firearm. It hinders and hence infringes the seller's rights.

The same logic applies to the buyer. The buyer's ability to keep and bear arms is certainly "infringed" by regulations that hinder the purchase of arms. After all, the Supreme Court has explained that inherent in "property" is the "right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." In other words, a restriction on the sale of weapons obviously impacts the buyer's constitutional rights to acquire weapons. As one scholar has explained it:.

Industry observers note that because one cannot 'keep' or 'bear' something without acquiring it, the act of acquiring arms must be included in the Second Amendment's 'right to keep and bear arms.' This is true for the same reason that the right to speak would be largely ineffective if it did not include the right to engage in financial transactions that are the incidents of its exercise. For there comes a point at which the regulation of action intimately and unavoidably connected with a right is a regulation of the right itself.

According to recent reports, joseph G.S. Greenlee, The American Tradition of Self-Made Arms, 54 St. Mary's L.J. 35 (2023).

Industry observers note that this principle is not limited to the Second Amendment context. For example, consider the neighboring First Amendment. The Free Speech Clause "afford[s] the public access to discussion, debate, and the dissemination of information and ideas"—and thus clearly protects the right to sell and distribute speech, including speech written or produced by others. And it protects the recipient's right to receive information and ideas. Willis v. Town of Marshall (9th Cir. 2002) (Kozinski, J., concurring) ("[T]he right to hear and the right to speak are flip sides of the same coin."). Without a right to provide speech, there is no right to receive information and ideas.

Likewise, consider the Free Exercise Clause. "[T]he text of the Free Exercise Clause gives a specific group of people (those who wish to engage in the 'exercise of religion') the right to do so without hindrance." It is axiomatic that the right to free exercise of religion includes the right to practice it with others in, for example, houses of worship. Shutting down houses of worship is an obvious First Amendment violation for many reasons—not the least of which is that it prevents the faithful from communing with each other and with church leaders who provide teaching, holy sacraments, and other sacred traditions. Thus, the right to exercise religion includes a First Amendment freedom to participate in religious services with—and provide religious services to—others.

Recent findings suggest that these examples demonstrate clear principles. A right to property, free speech, corporate worship, and firearms includes the right to provide these things. And to acquire them….

According to recent reports, judge Oldham also discussed the proper scope of a Fifth Circuit decision, U.S. v. Peterson (5th Cir. 2025) and concludes that it (1) "was wrong and should be overturned" and in any event (2) doesn't apply here; for more on that, read the full opinion.

Judge Catharina Haynes dissented:.

Sources indicate that I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered by the Second Amendment (which doesn't mention sellers) …. {Second Amendment is quite different from the First Amendment mentioned in the concurrence. The First Amendment states "freedom of speech" and lists people in general which is quite large whereas the Second Amendment claims "the right of people to keep and bear Arms" not mentioning selling Arms or all situations.}.

Recent findings suggest that [But] I am respectful of the majority opinion on that given our prior cases and what the government mentioned. So, even assuming arguendo the sellers are covered, I see nothing in this case that indicates that the rules for the sellers in this context are inappropriate and, therefore, unconstitutional. Also, to me, since Deare did not properly challenge the relevant rules to show that they are abusive, I do not see a need to remand on that. To me, the relevant rules as to him are sufficient and proper, so I would simply affirm.

I appreciate Judge Ho's and Judge Oldham's arguments that the right to keep and bear arms must include the right to acquire them, which in turn means that restrictions on sales must be evaluated to make sure they don't improperly burden the rights of would-be buyers. By way of analogy, the Court continues to recognize a right to use contraceptives (see Griswold v. Connecticut). Surely that must mean that a ban on selling contraceptives would unconstitutionally burden the would-be buyers' rights, and even less comprehensive restrictions on selling them might likewise be seen as too burdensome.

According to recent reports, but I'm skeptical of the argument that the Second Amendment secures a right of sellers independent of the right of buyers. A bookseller may be noted to be engaged in "speech" in the sense that conveying ideas to readers is a form of speech (including when one conveys them in exchange for money). A gun seller, on the other hand, isn't actually "keeping" a gun or "bearing" it. And though property rights do generally include the right to convey, including by sale, I don't think the Second Amendment should be seen as constitutionalizing that.

By way of analogy, the law bans transferring guns to felons. That, the Court has said, is presumptively constitutional, because felons don't have the right to possess guns (focusing on the rights of the would-be gun possessor). But I don't think it follows that the law even implicates the right of gun sellers. When the law bans me from selling a gun to a felon, it isn't affecting my own ability to keep or bear the gun at all.

Sources indicate that and this distinction between (1) the Second Amendment protecting gun sales as facilitative of the buyer's ability to have a gun, and (2) the Second Amendment gun sales as protecting the seller's own Second Amendment rights, may be practically significant. Under theory 1, there would likely be more room for regulation of sellers, since restrictions that only very modestly affect the buyer's ability to buy guns might then be viewed as presumptively constitutional. (That's consistent with D.C. v. Heller's statement that "nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on … laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms"). Under theory 2, there would be less room for regulation of sellers, since the sellers' own rights would be at stake as well.

According to recent reports, again, that's also how the distinction might play out as to the right to use contraceptives, and how it played out as to abortion in the pre-Dobbs Roe/Casey era. For instance, the right to abortion was consistent with licensure requirements for people or organizations that perform abortions, so long as this didn't unduly interfere with women's ability to get abortions. Likewise, it seems to me, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms is consistent with licensure requirements for gun sellers, so long as it doesn't unduly interfere with people's ability to get guns that they can then keep and bear.

#113817. Latest Update: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1711 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today, in Texas v.
  • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
  • During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

Industry observers note that the State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

The district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

Industry observers note that we conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

The enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

In a recent development, through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

Judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and new parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

It has been revealed that on May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

According to recent reports, 1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

According to recent reports, H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

According to recent reports, section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

Industry observers note that at problem here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

Industry observers note that even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

Recent findings suggest that after the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

The $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

It has been revealed that texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a newly introduced requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

According to recent reports, I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

The petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the newly introduced Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

David Beckham poses after he was made a knight bachelor at an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle on Nov. 4, 2025, in Windsor, England. (Photo by Andrew Matthews/Getty Images).

A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a New York court to dismiss the case.

The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the New York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another tech giant.

DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint remarked. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

Coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent company, declined to comment to the AP.

Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things.
  • Sources indicate that tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology.
  • According to recent reports, both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

It has been revealed that A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

Sources indicate that tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

According to recent reports, both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

Recent findings suggest that A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

According to recent reports, they give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, issue an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

Recent findings suggest that A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

“Each office knows the local area and will issue Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”.

Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can glitch one before snow or ice begins falling.

A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

In a recent development, A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

“Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

Recent findings suggest that once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

According to recent reports, if the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

It has been revealed that residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

According to recent reports, national Weather Service, “Winter Weather Warnings, Watches and Advisories” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Resources and Frequently Asked Questions” National Weather Service, “Prepare! Don’t Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise” Federal Emergency Management Agency, “Be Prepared for a Winter Storm”.

It has been revealed that last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”.

Industry observers note that fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

According to recent reports, the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

Recent findings suggest that it drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

It has been revealed that the short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

Recent findings suggest that I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

Sources indicate that there were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

Second, the depth drifted. After every 20 or 30 staples, I’d notice they were no longer seating at the depth I’d set and were starting to sit proud. I don’t know if that was due to denser 2x4s or inconsistencies between strips of staples, but it was something to keep an eye on. When I noticed it, I’d add a few clicks on the depth knob.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

In a recent development, A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The tool alone retails at The Home Depot for $119, but for the last few months, there’s been a special buy that includes the tool, a charger, and a 2.0 Ah Ridgid battery for $104.

Ridgid is owned by Emerson Electric Co., which makes the red Ridgid plumbing and pipe tools directly. The orange Ridgid cordless power tools, including this stapler, are made by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the company behind Milwaukee and Ryobi, under a licensing agreement with Emerson.

No. Staple guns need staples that match the tool’s crown width, leg length, and wire gauge. The Ridgid 18V crown stapler takes 3/8-in. crown staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long, including standard T50 staples. Other staplers may use different types, like narrow-crown or other heavy-duty series, so check the tool or the manual before you buy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I may not live in Ohio anymore, but there are some Ohio legal news stories I continue to follow. Here's one.

It has been revealed that soon-to-be-former Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) sued his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno), for defamation. Now that suit has been dismissed, and arguably in the worst way for Miller: The court concluded that the core underlying allegation is "substantially true.".

Miller filed the suit after the Daily Mail published a story reporting that Miller "hurled a pot of boiling water" at Moreno during an argument, and later wrote a note apologizing for the incident. As the court notes, an audio recording (that Miller released somehow thinking it would exonerate him) confirms the core of the claim. From the opinion:.

Industry observers note that an audio recording of the parties discussing the incident supports Defendant Moreno's contention of truth. Defendant Moreno confronted Plaintiff about pouring "bowling hot water on me." Although Plaintiff denies pouring hot water on her neck, he further admits the incident occurred. Plaintiff specifically stated "it was never done to hurt you with intent." Plaintiffs intent is irrelevant to the basic fact of whether the incident occurred, which addresses the element of falsity.

Plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is "categorically different" than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiffs burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.

The court also noted the lack of any evidence that Moreno was responsible for the Daily Mail's publication of the claims.

The court dismissed Miller's suit with prejudice and awarded costs and attorney fees. Additional litigation arising out of the Miller-Moreno divorce is pending, and it's always possible Miller will appeal. Moreno is not the first woman to accuse Miller of abuse.

More background from the Washington Post here.

[Note: As initially posted, I referred to Miller as "Former Rep. Miller." Of course, he is not yet a former representative, as his term has not yet ended, so I have updated the post accordingly.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward.
  • Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

It depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:.

It has been revealed that “Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”.

Industry observers note that another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.
