    Electrical tape comes in plenty of colors, but each has a purpose. Here's what the common shades mean in U.S. electrical work.

    Being a DIY electrician is one way homeowners like to save a little money over expensive repairs. However, there are safety concerns when it comes to doing your own electrical work. Electrical tape color meanings help electricians identify wires and make sense of connections that might otherwise look identical. The trouble is that colors don’t always mean the same thing.

    Learn what the common colors usually mean, how electricians use them, and why a strip of tape can’t confirm a wire’s purpose.

    According to recent reports, electricians use colored tape to identify wires, especially when several look alike. In the United States, the colors commonly mean:.

    In a recent development, these colors aren’t universal. The National Electrical Code sets rules for identifying neutral and grounding wires, but most hot-wire colors follow common practices rather than strict requirements. For example, orange can have a specific meaning in certain commercial electrical systems. Its purpose depends on the wiring, so electricians can’t rely on color alone.

    Industry observers note that electricians often wrap colored tape around the ends of wires to tell them apart. Manufacturers such as 3M make tape specifically for identifying different electrical connections.

    Tape can also show when a wire serves a different purpose than its original color suggests. For example, electricians may mark a white wire with black tape to identify it as a hot wire in certain situations. Electrical codes limit when and how they can make these changes.

    It has been revealed that however, tape color alone can’t confirm a wire’s purpose or whether it carries electricity. Previous repairs, incorrect markings, or different labeling practices can cause confusion. Before starting electrical work, a qualified person should identify the circuit and test that the power is off. Homeowners who encounter unfamiliar or conflicting wire markings should have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring.

    • A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors.
    • Sources indicate that whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause.
    • Cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors. Here's why cities give them out and what recipients actually receive.

    Sources indicate that whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause. But what does the key actually do?

    Cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize. Learn what a key to the city represents, how the custom began, and what someone actually gets to do with it.

    A key to the city is an award that cities give to people they want to honor.

    “The Key to the City is presented as a symbol of civic recognition and Philadelphia’s appreciation for individuals whose achievements, service and influence have made a meaningful impact on the city and its people,” according to a release from the City of Philadelphia.

    The key is usually decorative, with the city’s name or seal on it. Some come in a display box or with a certificate. Little Rock, Arkansas, considers its key the city’s highest ceremonial honor.

    But the key won’t open City Hall or any other public building. It doesn’t give the recipient special privileges or any authority, either. In 2010, Fresh York City tried something different with an art project that gave people working keys to certain locations. Those weren’t the same as the city’s usual honorary keys.

    The tradition goes back to when cities had walls and gates that closed at night. Giving someone a key meant they could come and go without asking permission.

    In medieval Europe, leaders also exchanged keys during official visits or military surrenders. Handing over the keys sometimes meant giving up control of a city. Over time, the custom became a way to welcome or honor someone.

    Industry observers note that today, cities give keys to athletes, public figures, volunteers, and local residents. Each city has its own rules for who receives one.

    According to recent reports, philadelphia, for example, honored a resident in 2026 after he walked across the country to support career opportunities for young people. Elk Grove, California, recognizes military accomplishments and acts of heroism, while Little Rock reserves its keys for people who live outside Arkansas.

    Mayors usually present the keys, although some cities involve the city council or accept nominations from residents. Recipients get a keepsake and some public recognition, but no special privileges.

    Second Amendment Roundup: AR-15 Film Redux.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Smith released his new 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle.
    • That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising.
    • As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his new 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago. The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

    That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument. The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

    As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film. From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

    Sources indicate that but there is another key aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

    The animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics. Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:.

    Industry observers note that there is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition. This is called autoloading. This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those fresh to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

    The film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark indicates an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

    The film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

    It has been revealed that animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round. The film's animation shows the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

    Recent findings suggest that the film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning. Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things. The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

    According to recent reports, it has been stated that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's new film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice.
    • According to recent reports, navigating a upcoming parking lot can be confusing and stressful.
    • Sources indicate that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

    According to recent reports, navigating a upcoming parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

    Sources indicate that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

    Recent findings suggest that diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

    In a recent development, drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

    Not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”.

    It has been revealed that the benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

    There’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

    In a recent development, some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”.

    In a recent development, back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

    Industry News: 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.
    • Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
    • Recent findings suggest that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

    Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

    Recent findings suggest that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

    Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

    In a recent development, ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

    De-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy claims.

    According to recent reports, though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

    Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

    Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

    It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

    “New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

    “Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy indicates.

    All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher says.

    According to recent reports, natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

    Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

    Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

    Sources indicate that ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

    Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

    Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

    Sources indicate that electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

    Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice swiftly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

    “The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher indicates, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

    Sources indicate that regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy indicates. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

    Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

    According to recent reports, it depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher states, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

    Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher notes, as they still contain salt.

    The Safest Way to Shovel Snow, According to Experts

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.
    • Sources indicate that with autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months.
    • Recent findings suggest that shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

    Sources indicate that with autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not fresh to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

    Recent findings suggest that shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

    It has been revealed that the safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

    “The most vital tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer says. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

    Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

    Recent findings suggest that consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

    In a recent development, snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to swiftly remove snow without any manual input.

    Keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

    “It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer states. That’s why it’s vital to pace yourself, stop regularly and blueprint ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will quickly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

    Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

    “Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer indicates. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

    It has been revealed that dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

    “It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

    Sources indicate that shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

    It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

    Recent findings suggest that individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

    What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks.
    • According to recent reports, drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in.
    • Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    In a recent development, those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

    According to recent reports, drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

    Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

    Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

    In a recent development, rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

    It has been revealed that drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

    Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

    It has been revealed that drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

    More serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

    Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

    Federal Highway Administration, “Questions and Answers About Vehicle Size and Weight” Federal Highway Administration, “Truck Size and Weight Enforcement Technologies, WIM Technology Overview” Federal Highway Administration, “Compliance Comparative Analysis Technical Report, Compliance Effectiveness of Enforcement” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Inspections” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Out-of-Service Criteria”.

    #113766. Industry News: Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1208 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.
    • In this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night.
    • Recent findings suggest that liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Croteau v. Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.

    In this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night. The summary judgment rested on the circuit court's application of "the dram shop statute"—section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020):.

    Recent findings suggest that liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication. A person who sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person of lawful drinking age shall not thereby become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such person, except that a person who willfully and unlawfully sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person who is not of lawful drinking age or who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such minor or person.

    In a recent development, the underlined second exception is at matter here…. In addressing "what constitutes 'knowledge' in order for a vendor's conduct to be found negligent," the [Florida Supreme Court has] found:.

    [T]he cause of action [under section 768.125's second exception] only requires evidence that the vendor had knowledge that the individual the vendor served was a habitual drunkard. Serving an individual multiple drinks on one occasion would be insufficient, in and of itself, to establish that the vendor knowingly served a habitual drunkard alcoholic beverages. On the other hand, serving an individual a substantial number of drinks on multiple occasions would be circumstantial evidence to be considered by the jury in determining whether the vendor knew that the person was a habitual drunkard….

    It has been revealed that [In another case,] we affirmed a summary judgment for the defendant bar, where the plaintiff patron was unknown to the bar's staff, was not a bar regular, and had purchased up to four drinks over two to three hours. We held that we could not impute notice of the patron's alcohol addiction to the bar when the patron had not shown any signs of intoxication, despite his alcohol consumption ….

    Here, consistent with [those precedents], the bar's serving the alcoholic beverages to the plaintiff for the first time on the incident date, without more, should not be considered sufficient evidence to impute knowledge to the bar that the plaintiff was "habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages." ….

    It has been revealed that roster v. Moulton (Fla. App. 1992)—the primary case upon which the plaintiff relies—is distinguishable….

    Industry observers note that [In Roster,] [i]t is undisputed that [the patron] consumed 8–10, 12–ounce cans of beer and two straight shots of tequila over the period of an hour and a half. After a short absence from [the bar], during which [the patron] drank yet another beer served elsewhere, [the patron] returned to [the bar's] walk-up window, where he ordered and was served another beer. The [bar manager] admitted that it would be unusual for a person to consume that many beers and two shots of tequila without showing signs of intoxication. Despite [the patron's] considerable alcohol consumption, [the patron] did not stagger and did not slur his speech. The manager twice asked [the patron] to leave the bar only because [the patron] became loud and argumentative. [The patron] pled guilty to the charge of driving while under the influence of alcohol and admitted that he had a drinking problem from the age of sixteen, which he still had at the time of the accident. At that time, [the patron] had never received treatment for his alcohol addiction….

    In a recent development, by affidavit in Roster, "two experts[] … essentially stated that the large amount of alcohol that [the patron had] consumed over a relatively short time period, together with the lack of impairment [which the patron had] demonstrated, would have put a reasonable server of alcohol on notice that [the patron] was habitually addicted to alcohol. [The bar] submitted no affidavits to oppose these viewpoints." ….

    However, unlike in Roster, as the bar's answer brief submits:.

    In a recent development, … [W]hatever alcohol [the plaintiff] may have consumed at [the bar], she claims she drank over a five-hour period—much longer than the 90 minutes during which the Roster [patron] consumed 10–12 drinks. Furthermore, [the plaintiff] claims she sat, ordered drink(s), and watched television for five hours, which is much different than the Roster [patron,] who left the bar …, drank another alcoholic beverage elsewhere, and then came back to the bar where he was served yet another drink. Also, unlike … in Roster, there is no evidence that [the plaintiff] demonstrated a level of intoxication consistent with someone who had either a high or low tolerance for alcohol. Finally, unlike the [patron] in Roster, [the plaintiff here] did not become loud or argumentative at the [bar]. By her own admission, she was quiet, not boisterous, not loud, not abusive, and she simply kept to herself….

    Unlike the Roster patron, the plaintiff here was an anonymous patron, whose behavior during her visit to the bar was, by her own statements, unremarkable.

    Judge Lott agreed, but added that he thought Roster was wrongly decided, including in its reliance on expert evidence:.

    Section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020), says that a bar owner is not liable for damage caused by the sale of alcoholic beverages, except that (as relevant here) a person "who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable." The language does not require expert testimony, and does not ask how the latest version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) defines pathologies related to alcohol use….

    In a recent development, the statutory language asks whether the server has actual knowledge that the person is, as a matter of habit, addicted to alcohol…. You know such a thing when you see it—and it's hard to imagine being able to see it given only a single occasion of indulgence…. [A]nyone can have too many drinks. What separates a "habitual drunkard" [which is how the concurrence elsewhere interprets "habitually addicted"] is that the habitual drunkard feels compelled to do so on account of their addiction, and does so regularly as a matter of habit….

    According to recent reports, turning back to Roster—where was the evidence that the defendant actually knew that the plaintiff was habitually addicted to alcohol? The defendant observed the plaintiff drink heavily on one occasion wherein he handled his liquor well, until he didn't. No evidence of "addiction" was presented, much less of a "habit" of it. The expert affidavits about his apparent alcohol tolerance added nothing to that inquiry.

    Industry observers note that in sum, Roster passed the buck from the statutory language to expert opinion, and reached the wrong result in turn. In an appropriate case, we should consider whether to recede from it….

    Jack R. Reiter and Robert C. Weill (GrayRobinson, P.A.) represent the bar.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

    Recent findings suggest that the holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

    Sources indicate that A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

    Learn what a roofing expert claims about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

    A post shared by Drew (@thedrewsocial).

    Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing firm in Illinois.

    Recent findings suggest that “That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski states. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create concerns with moisture.”.

    The cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

    Recent findings suggest that chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

    According to recent reports, rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski says.

    In a recent development, wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

    Sources indicate that moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”.

    A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

    In a recent development, homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

    In a recent development, roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

    Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

    Sources indicate that for homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

    If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

    Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    California ordered Waymo off freeways after troubling encounters with road crews and police. Here's what happened and how riders are affected.

    Driving through a construction zone can be confusing, especially when lanes are closed or police are directing traffic. Waymo’s self-driving cars have run into problems in these situations, too.

    On Nov. 11, California banned Waymo from operating driverless vehicles on freeways following several incidents involving road crews and police. The manufacturer has since stopped freeway rides in other states as well.

    Here’s why California stepped in and what the ban means for Waymo passengers.

    The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) remarked the incidents put construction workers and other drivers at risk.

    On Nov. 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near Burlingame, where crews were working. Waymo mentioned no one was injured, and no collisions occurred.

    The next day, another Waymo attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles during a traffic break on Interstate 280. Officers use traffic breaks to slow or stop vehicles, often because of roadwork or a hazard ahead. Drivers must stay behind the patrol cars until officers allow traffic to resume.

    Waymo had similar problems in May, which led to a temporary suspension and software changes. But latest incidents occurred in November.

    According to recent reports, in April, California approved stricter rules for self-driving cars. DMV Director Steve Gordon remarked the changes would bring “additional accountability for AV manufacturers.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the freeway ban doesn’t affect Waymo’s regular street service, although some trips may take longer. Waymo has also voluntarily stopped commercial freeway rides in other states while it looks into what went wrong.

    Waymo’s cars use cameras and sensors to monitor traffic, but construction zones don’t always follow normal traffic patterns. The recent incidents demonstrated problems with how the vehicles responded to road closures and police activity.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s no date yet for Waymo to return to California freeways. The DMV wants the company to show that its cars can safely handle road closures and police activity before allowing driverless freeway rides again.

    Waymo notes it’s working with state officials and will continue testing on freeways with trained specialists behind the wheel. Passengers can still book rides on regular streets in the meantime.

    Has Congress Learned How To Conduct Effective Oversight?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability.
    • According to recent reports, listening to some talk about their plans, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think.
    • In a recent development, I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability. They have also pledged to engage in extensive oversight and investigation of the Trump Administration, and firms and individuals that have operated within the White House's orbit.

    According to recent reports, listening to some talk about their plans, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think. The authority to conduct inquiries for legislative purposes is broad, but it has limits. And during the first Trump Administration, the failure of House Democrats to contend with those limits hampered oversight efforts.

    In a recent development, I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column. In this piece, I explain why Trump v. Mazars is the greater constraint on free-wheeling fishing expeditions than is the Trump immunity decision.

    Sources indicate that nothing in the Constitution expressly grants Congress the power to investigate executive branch agencies, let alone the President (or anyone else, for that matter). The authority to conduct oversight is an adjunct to Congress's legislative powers. In the simplest terms, it is often necessary and proper for Congress to secure information and conduct inquiries as it considers legislation and makes appropriation decisions. Or, as the Court explained in Mazars, this "power of inquiry—with process to enforce it—is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function." , , ,.

    Industry observers note that no justice in Mazars endorsed the then-common view that Congress could demand all information it sought, subject only to the constraints imposed by Executive Privilege. Rather, the justices were unanimous that Congress lacks the power to investigate for investigation's sake, or to conduct oversight for the purpose of public disclosure or inducing prosecution. Congress has no authority to try private citizens in a committee hearing. As the Chief Justice explained in his opinion for the Court, congressional subpoenas are valid only insofar as they are "related to, and in furtherance of, a legitimate task of the Congress." More generally, congressional subpoenas must serve "a valid legislative purpose," and Congress bears the burden of demonstrating this standard is met. Document demands that appear designed more to harass or punish the political opposition than to inform legitimate legislative activity will not be enforced.

    Insofar as Congress wishes to investigate the White House or high-ranking officials, its greatest investigatory authority is not the power to inquire for legislative purposes. Rather, it is the power to impeach. In practice, this means some of the greater restraints on Congressional oversight are political, rather than legal.

    While the Court's decision in Mazars focused on the connection between document demands and the legislative process, this is not the only path Congress may take. The Constitution grants Congress the power to enact legislation for various purposes. It also delegates the power to impeach, and these powers are distinct. As Judge Neomi Rao explained when the Mazars case was before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, "investigations of impeachable offenses simply are not, and never have been, within Congress's legislative power." They stand on their own bottom.

    Industry observers note that this distinction matters, because if Congress wishes to investigate potentially impeachable offenses, it must be clear that is what it is doing so voters can evaluate its actions accordingly. "Allowing Congress to investigate impeachable officials for suspicions of criminality pursuant to the legislative power has serious consequences for the separation of powers because it allows Congress to escape the responsibility and accountability inherent in impeachment proceedings," Judge Rao warned. This wolf must come as a wolf.

    According to recent reports, and on Trump v. U.S., I take a different view than some other legal commentators:.

    Some commentators fear that the Supreme Court's presidential immunity decision in Trump v. United States will hamper otherwise legitimate congressional inquiries. "Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the President's actions on subjects within his 'conclusive and preclusive' constitutional authority," the Court declared. While this insulates the President from criminal prosecution for actions within the core of executive authority and would accordingly limit the Congress' ability to subpoena related information for legislative oversight purposes, it is no shield in matters of impeachment.

    Industry observers note that aggressive Congressional oversight of the executive branch is not fresh. Nor is the politicization of oversight. Once political parties emerged, it was inevitable that party loyalty would rival (if not overcome) each branch's institutional imperatives. Oversight fights were once more political than legal, but Congress could also defend its prerogatives without invoking the courts. A Congress that legislates and appropriates through regular order has more weapons to deploy and a greater ability to force executive branch acquiescence. Insofar as the next round of oversight fights are resolved in court, it will be yet another sign of Congress's decline.

    For a deeper dive, my Cato Supreme Court Review article on the Mazars and Vance decisions is here.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta’s repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country’s judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses.

    Burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo unveiled on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry, Issaka Lingani, Inoussa Ouédraogo, Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry, and international journalist Wassim Nasr. They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

    Burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d’Ivoire, France, and the United States, said Sawadogo. He added that Burkina Faso asked the United States to use Meta to identify and prosecute Facebook page administrators accused of promoting terrorism.

    It has been revealed that the authorities are using counterterrorism laws to target critical voices and restrict independent reporting on military abuses. The extradition requests extend political repression beyond Burkina Faso’s borders, placing critics who sought protection abroad at risk of arrest, forced return, and further abuse. The government’s recent decision to reinstate capital punishment for offenses including terrorism, high treason, and espionage is also of grave concern.

    Since seizing power in a September 2022 coup, the junta has restricted fundamental rights through media bans, suspension of unions and civil society organizations, dissolution of political parties, enforced disappearances, and the unlawful conscription of government critics.

    Meanwhile, the conflict between government forces and allied militias and Islamist armed groups, ongoing since 2017, has involved widespread abuses by all parties, including war crimes and crimes against humanity, with no accountability. Human Rights Watch has documented serious flaws in the special terrorism court, including prolonged pretrial detention, and violations of fair trial guarantees.

    Concerned governments should rigorously scrutinize all extradition and judicial cooperation requests from Burkina Faso. No journalist, activist or political opponent should be returned where there are substantial grounds to fear torture, arbitrary detention, an unfair trial, and the death penalty. International partners should condemn the targeting of critics at home and abroad and reject Burkina Faso’s attempts at transnational repression.

(8) disseminating any videotape, photograph, film or image of another identifiable person 18 years of age or older who is nude or engaged in sexual activity and under circumstances in which such identifiable person had a reasonable expectation of privacy, with the intent to harass, threaten or intimidate such identifiable person, and such identifiable person did not consent to such dissemination." ….

    The court held White didn't violate the statute:.

    Here Sarah consented to the photos being taken and the video being made. White later emailed and texted the sexually explicit material only to Sarah. How did that conduct breach Sarah's privacy? ….

    Sarah had an expectation of privacy as to the photos and the video to the extent that she could reasonably expect that no one other than she and White would ever see the sexually explicit images. White did not violate that expectation of privacy.

    In a recent development, the evidence showed that White transmitted the sexually explicit material to Sarah with the intent to harass her. But for there to be a breach of privacy under [the statute], the term "disseminating" requires that the illicit material be sent to someone other than the person depicted in the material and who consented to the illicit material being made. White's conduct here more than likely constituted harassment by telecommunication device in violation of K.S.A. 21-6206, but we find it did not constitute breach of privacy….

    #113757. "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1276 w)

    "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I'm serializing my latest Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.
    • Throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels.
    • According to recent reports, yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I'm serializing my latest Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.

    Throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels. The first precedent on this was Brandreth v. Lance (1839), an 1839 Newly introduced York trial court decision. This was followed by State ex rel. Liversey v. Judge (1882), an 1882 Louisiana Supreme Court decision. Subsequent decisions helped establish this as a firm rule, seemingly culminating in Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson.

    According to recent reports, yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels. By my count the court systems of thirty-four states have either so held or have in practice been so acting, with only six states plus D.C. continuing to categorically bar such injunctions. {See Eugene Volokh, Anti-Libel Injunctions, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 73 (2019).}.

    This trend seems to have accelerated with the rise of the internet. Historically, a libel has been a short, sharp shock—typically, a one-time article in a newspaper that is printed and can't be removed—with the only possible remedy being damages or criminal prosecution. But the internet can turn libel into a steady drip, drip, drip of damage, with more readers seeing a libelous web page every day. Injunctions thus seem a more useful remedy.

    The internet also makes it easier for judgment-proof defendants to cause real damage; an injunction can thus be useful in a way that a damages remedy might not be. Criminal libel is theoretically available in about ten states, and there are indeed likely a couple of dozen criminal libel prosecutions in the United States each year. But in most states the only way to deploy criminal remedies in service of protecting reputation is through getting an injunction that can be enforced through the threat of criminal contempt.

    Are these injunctions contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment? The answer turns out to be complicated, especially if we focus on permanent injunctions, entered to forbid the repetition of material found to be libelous in a final judgment (with the defendant having had an opportunity to call for a jury trial).

    It's true that early sources often view the freedom of the press as precluding prior restraints: To quote William Blackstone, "The liberty of the press is indeed essential to the nature of a free state: but this consists in laying no previous restraints upon publications, and not in freedom from censure for criminal matter when published." Yet this doesn't quite speak to the modern question whether the law may restrain repetition of material for matter found to be criminal (or tortious).

    In a recent development, nor does it speak to whether the law may require removal of such matter after a trial: Removal just wasn't practically an option in the print era. In such situations of injunctions against repetition of an already published libel or ordering its removal, "[e]very freeman" would retain the "undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases before the public" (again quoting Blackstone) at least in the first instance.

    Recent findings suggest that nor is there a "restrictive power of a licenser" or "control of an inspector" in the sense that the Framers likely understood licensers, which is to say officials administering a licensing system. (To quote St. George Tucker, under that system "all books printed were previously licensed by some of the great offices of state, or the two universities, and all foreign books were exposed to a similar scrutiny before they were vended.") The injunction is imposed by a judge, often following a jury verdict, administering justice between two parties, not running a traditional licensing system that "subject[s] all freedom of sentiment to the prejudices of one man, and make[s] him the arbitrary and infallible judge of all controverted points in learning, religion, and government.".

    According to recent reports, likewise, early sources stressed the importance of allowing a jury to resolve what is true and false in libel cases. But, as I noted, the modern permanent injunction in libel cases is entered after a final judgment on the merits, which at least in principle allows a defendant to demand a jury trial. If the defendant has so demanded, then any injunction would be based on the jury verdict.

    Industry observers note that this stems in part from the twentieth-century merger of law and equity, since equitable remedies, such as injunctions, can now be issued following the use of the legal procedure of a jury trial. (Historically, one argument against injunctions in libel cases has been that "equity will not enjoin a libel," a statement about the limits of the equity courts more than about constitutional protections for free expression.) Indeed, the Delaware Court of Chancery, which operates in a state system where law and equity remain largely separate, has continued to hold that it generally can't enjoin libel. But it expressly left open the possibility that, once the Delaware Superior Court (the law court) concludes—after a jury trial, if the parties don't choose a bench trial—that a statement is libelous, an injunction can then be issued.

    In practice, anti-libel injunctions are often parts of default judgments, or follow bench trials, and thus don't involve factual findings by juries. In both those situations, though, the defendant can be said to have waived his right to a jury trial. To be sure, temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are entered before any opportunity for a jury trial—but for that reason many courts continue to reject them on First Amendment grounds.

    And, as the California Supreme Court held in allowing such post-final-judgment permanent injunctions, the reasoning of Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson expressly sets aside injunctions in traditional civil libel disputes:.

    The high court was careful to point out … that the statute being considered was "not aimed at the redress of individual or private wrongs. Remedies for libel remain available and unaffected." … But most significant is that the court … clarified that it was not addressing "questions as to the extent of authority to prevent publications in order to protect private rights according to the principles governing the exercise of the jurisdiction of courts of equity." In a footnote, the court cited [an] … article by Roscoe Pound that observed that English courts permit "an injunction in case the libel was repeated or publication was continued after a jury had found the matter libelous." Therefore, Near expressly did not address the matter posed in the present case.

    The Supreme Court hasn't confronted such permanent injunctions against repetition of proven libel since Near, but it has authorized injunctions against obscenity (which Near had anticipated) and against commercial speech that proposes illegal transactions. The one case in which it granted certiorari as to anti-libel injunctions, Tory v. Cochran (2005), largely disappeared when the plaintiff, famed lawyer Johnnie Cochran, died while the case was pending. None of these cases discussed the original meaning of the First Amendment, and the lower court cases dealing with the matter have largely not discussed it, either.

    Sources indicate that so here we have a fairly rich body of originalist evidence related to libel law generally. We have a considerable body of evidence from before and shortly after the Framing that talks about "previous restraints." And we have some nineteenth-century sources that seem to take the view that all injunctions in libel cases are unconstitutional. But how exactly do the Framing-era sources apply to a permanent anti-libel injunction issued by a court following the resolution of a libel case? Hard to know for sure.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Fresh York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

    Rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights in 2002, later becoming its president, and co-founded and was executive director of the Gulf Centre for Human Rights starting in 2011.

    Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

    Bahraini authorities unjustly detained and imprisoned him several times for his peaceful expression in the years following the 2011 pro-democracy protests in Bahrain. In 2018, he was sentenced to five years in prison for his comments criticizing torture at a Bahraini prison and the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. Even from detention, he continued his activism. In 2017, he wrote an op-ed for the Newly introduced York Times from detention, titled “Don’t Profit from Abuses by Bahrain,” calling out US support of Bahraini authorities despite their abuses both in Bahrain and amid the conflict in Yemen. He wrote:.

    All our destinies are tied together. What will happen to Bahrain if everyone who supports peace, democracy and the rule of law is in jail? To whom will Bahrain’s disenfranchised youth turn to for support and guidance? These are the questions the Trump administration must ask itself before it sends my jailers another batch of fighter jets.

    Recent findings suggest that he was released from prison in 2020 and allowed to serve the rest of his sentence at home with his family, but only after his health deteriorated due to harsh detention conditions. In the years that followed, he continued to support the human rights movement and call out human rights abuses by Bahraini and other authorities across the world.

    Sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, the advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and a close friend, said that Rajab left Bahrain in March 2026 so that he could speak publicly on Bahraini human rights issues. He remained in exile until his passing, unable to return to Bahrain for fear of being rearrested.

    Rajab’s death is a profound blow to the global and Arab human rights movements, which have lost a steadfast defender of freedom of expression and a voice of reason in a climate increasingly marked by hatred and polarization. Over many years, Rajab stood resolutely by his principles, despite being targeted, detained, and repressed for his unwavering commitment to universal human rights.

    Sources indicate that “Nabeel was a stalwart champion for human rights and democracy, not just for Bahrain but all of the Middle East,” remarked Sarah Leah Whitson, former Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He paid a tremendous price for his advocacy, jailed and abused in prison, but always kept us hopeful and resilient. He played an essential role in guiding and supporting the work of Human Rights Watch’s MENA division. I considered him a true friend.”.

    According to recent reports, “Nabeel’s legacy lives on in the innumerable people he inspired, fought alongside in the defense of rights, and held up, sometimes in their darkest moments,” said Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He has been a leader and guide to human rights defenders in the region. He and his family paid a high price for his activism, but we are grateful for his wisdom, tenacity, and courage.”.

    In a recent development, nabeel Rajab’s courage, integrity, and principled advocacy will be his enduring legacy. Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and the many friends who mourn his loss.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm.
    • The motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of Fresh York on September 29, 2025.
    • On September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the Fresh York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From a N.Y. appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm. v. Fernich (Judges Sallie Manzanet-Daniels, Tanya R. Kennedy, Barbara R. Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent Newly introduced York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):.

    The motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of Fresh York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

    On September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the Fresh York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine.".

    Sources indicate that respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

    Among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also stated that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

    Sources indicate that at his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

    He also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

    In a recent development, the parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

    Industry observers note that the record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical issues at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

    Recent findings suggest that under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

    Industry observers note that respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

    Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

    Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.
